title: Divine Mercy Sunday
hook: the second Sunday of Easter, named by John Paul II in 2000

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Easter octave: eight days kept as one. Your line was one long day. What small Easter thing did you keep going? Today is the octave's last day. Day six hundred sixty-six.

In a convent in Poland in the 1930s, a young nun with little schooling kept a notebook. Her name was Faustina Kowalska. She wrote that Jesus had appeared to her, robed in white, with two rays streaming from his heart, one pale and one red. She was asked to have the image painted, with a short line of trust underneath. She died of tuberculosis in 1938, at thirty-three. Sixty-two years later, in Rome, a Polish pope declared her a saint, and gave a name to the Sunday that ends the Easter octave.
screen: `A NOTEBOOK IN A POLISH CONVENT.` → `TWO RAYS, PALE AND RED.` → `A LINE UNDERNEATH.`

segments.voice: On the thirtieth of April, 2000, John Paul II canonized Faustina and announced that, from then on, the second Sunday of Easter would be called Divine Mercy Sunday across the whole Church. The Latin word for mercy, misericordia, joins the heart, cor, to someone's misery. The readings didn't change. The Gospel this Sunday, in every year of the cycle, is John 20: the risen Jesus walking through locked doors, breathing on the disciples, and saying, in the Douay-Rheims, "Receive ye the Holy Ghost. Whose sins you shall forgive, they are forgiven them." He greets frightened friends who ran away with peace, shows them his wounds, and then hands them the power to forgive. Then Thomas, who wasn't there, gets his own visit a week later, and Jesus says: "Blessed are they that have not seen, and have believed." So the feast's theme was already sitting in the text. Faustina's image puts it in a picture: in her diary, the two rays stand for the blood and water that flowed from his side. And the line at the bottom, in her Polish, is three words, Jezu, ufam Tobie. In English it's the line Catholics now pray: Jesus, I trust in you. A surprise: for about twenty years, the Vatican restricted this devotion, partly because of flawed copies of her writings. The restriction was lifted in 1978, the year a cardinal from Kraków, where she had lived, became pope. Catholics are free to take up Faustina's devotions or not; the Church approves them without requiring them. But the line itself is short enough for anyone to carry. In English, five words. Not I understand. Not I'm sure. Just trust.
screen: `NAMED ON 30 APRIL 2000.` · `THE GOSPEL: FORGIVE, AND THOMAS.` · `TWO RAYS: BLOOD AND WATER.` · `RESTRICTED, THEN LIFTED IN 1978.` · then, large: `BLESSED ARE THEY THAT HAVE NOT SEEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one short line, slowly. Sit and let your breathing settle. Think of one thing you're carrying that you can't fix today. Name it. Then, if you pray, say Faustina's line on your breath: Jesus, I trust in you. Breathe in on Jesus, out on the rest. Let it repeat for as long as the bell holds. If you don't pray, simply hold the worry in an open hand instead of a fist. The bell holds the time.
misericordia. The Latin word for mercy, joining heart to someone's misery, behind the feast John Paul II named in 2000, when he canonized Saint Faustina. Today's word.
Your line: Jesus, I trust in you. Today, when the worry you named comes back, say the line once, or simply open your hand. Day six hundred sixty-six.

howItsDone: On Divine Mercy Sunday Catholic parishes often display the Divine Mercy image, hear the Gospel of doubting Thomas from John 20, offer confession, and pray the Divine Mercy chaplet, often at three in the afternoon; the words Jesus, I trust in you are printed beneath the image.

notes: Faustina: born 1905, died 5 October 1938 aged 33; canonized 30 April 2000. Confirm.
The Holy Office notification restricting the devotion (1958/1959) and its reversal (1978); 'about twenty years' and reason 'partly flawed copies/translations' are common summaries; confirm framing.
John Paul II (Karol Wojtyła, archbishop of Kraków) elected October 1978; the 1978 lifting came in April, before his election; the script says 'the year', not 'by him'. Confirm.
Two rays (pale and red) interpreted as water and blood per Faustina's diary; confirm.
Polish inscription is 'Jezu, ufam Tobie'. Misericordia etymology (miser + cor) per standard Latin lexicons; confirm.

Editor review (2026-10-01): the inscription 'Jezu, ufam Tobie' is three words in Polish, so 'five words underneath' and 'the five words... in her Polish' were wrong; now 'a line' and 'in English, five words'. 'The very first thing he does... is hand them the power to forgive' skipped 'Peace be to you' and the wounds (John 20:19–20); teach and fork corrected. 'Has always been John 20' now 'in every year of the cycle'; 'hear the Gospel of Thomas' (which names an apocryphal text) now 'the Gospel of doubting Thomas from John 20'. Dates in the hook (died 1938 at thirty-three; canonized sixty-two years later) are kept; confirm against the canonization homily.
